questions.stem: In a mass spectrum, what is the base peak?
options: The peak at m/z zero, used as the reference point
The tallest peak, from the most abundant ion, set to 100%
The peak with the highest m/z, from the molecular ion
The peak with the lowest m/z, from the smallest fragment
questions.explanation: The base peak is the most intense peak in the spectrum, and other peak heights are given relative to it. The molecular ion peak, at the highest significant m/z, gives the molar mass and is often not the base peak.

questions.stem: The mass spectrum of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, has a molecular ion at m/z 46 and a large peak at m/z 31. Which ion produces the peak at m/z 31?
options: CH₂OH⁺
C₂H₅⁺
CH₃⁺
OH⁺
questions.explanation: Breaking the C-C bond of the molecular ion gives a CH₂OH⁺ fragment of mass 12 + 2 + 16 + 1 = 31. C₂H₅⁺ has m/z 29, CH₃⁺ has m/z 15 and OH⁺ has m/z 17.

questions.stem: A haloalkane's mass spectrum shows molecular ion peaks at m/z 64 and 66 in a 3 : 1 height ratio. Which compound is it?
options: Chloromethane, CH₃Cl
Dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂
Chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl
Bromoethane, C₂H₅Br
questions.explanation: Chlorine occurs as about three parts chlorine-35 to one part chlorine-37, so a compound with one Cl atom gives two molecular ion peaks 2 units apart in a 3 : 1 ratio. C₂H₅³⁵Cl has m/z 24 + 5 + 35 = 64. Bromine would give peaks of nearly equal height, and chloromethane would give 50 and 52.

questions.stem: A straight-chain alkane gives a molecular ion peak at m/z 86. What is its molecular formula?
options: C₅H₁₂
C₇H₁₆
C₆H₁₂
C₆H₁₄
questions.explanation: Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, so 12n + 2n + 2 = 86 gives n = 6 and the formula C₆H₁₄. C₆H₁₂ has m/z 84 and is not an alkane.

questions.stem: How can mass spectrometry measure the amount of a pesticide in a river water sample, as well as identify it?
options: Its fragment pattern identifies it; a key peak's size is compared with standards
Its molecular ion is weighed on a balance after it has been separated from the water sample
Its infrared absorptions are measured and compared with those of known pesticide solutions
Its boiling point is measured as it leaves the instrument, then compared with standards
questions.explanation: The pattern of fragment peaks acts as a fingerprint that is matched against reference spectra. The intensity of a characteristic peak increases with the amount of the compound, so comparing it with standards of known concentration gives a quantitative result.

questions.stem: An IR spectrum shows a broad absorption at 3230 to 3550 cm⁻¹ and no absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹. Which functional group is present?
options: Carbon-carbon double bond
Hydroxyl group of an alcohol
Carboxyl group of an acid
Ester group
questions.explanation: A broad band at 3230 to 3550 cm⁻¹ is due to the hydrogen-bonded O-H of an alcohol. A carboxylic acid would show a very broad O-H band at 2500 to 3000 cm⁻¹ and a strong C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹, and an ester would also show the C=O absorption.

questions.stem: Which feature of their IR spectra distinguishes but-1-ene from butane?
options: A broad absorption at 3230 to 3550 cm⁻¹ for O-H, present only for butane
An absorption at 2850 to 3000 cm⁻¹ for C-H, present only for but-1-ene
A strong absorption at 1700 cm⁻¹ for C=O, present only for butane
An absorption at 1620 to 1680 cm⁻¹ for C=C, present only for but-1-ene
questions.explanation: The C=C stretch absorbs at about 1620 to 1680 cm⁻¹, so only the alkene shows it. Both compounds contain C-H bonds, so both absorb near 2850 to 3000 cm⁻¹, and neither contains O-H or C=O.

questions.stem: What is the fingerprint region of an IR spectrum used for?
options: Measuring the molar mass of a compound from the position of its largest absorption
Counting the number of hydrogen environments in a molecule from the peak heights
Showing the O-H and C=O groups, which absorb only below 1500 cm⁻¹
Identifying a compound by matching its pattern to a reference spectrum
questions.explanation: Below about 1500 cm⁻¹ many overlapping absorptions give a pattern unique to each compound, so it is compared with reference spectra to confirm identity. The O-H and C=O absorptions lie above 1500 cm⁻¹, and IR does not give molar mass.

questions.stem: The IR spectrum of a petroleum fraction shows strong absorption at 2850 to 3000 cm⁻¹ only. After cracking, a new absorption appears at about 1650 cm⁻¹. What does this show?
options: The fraction was alkenes, and cracking has produced alkanes
The fraction contained alcohols, which cracking has oxidised
Cracking has produced carboxylic acids from the alkanes
The fraction was alkanes, and cracking has produced alkenes
questions.explanation: Absorption only from C-H bonds at 2850 to 3000 cm⁻¹ fits saturated hydrocarbons. The new band near 1650 cm⁻¹ is a C=C stretch, showing that cracking has formed alkenes. Alcohols or acids would show O-H bands, and acids also a C=O band.

questions.stem: What is crude oil (petroleum) mainly composed of?
options: A mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes
A single pure hydrocarbon, octane
A mixture of alcohols and carboxylic acids
A mixture of ionic compounds and water
questions.explanation: Petroleum is a complex mixture of many hydrocarbons, mainly alkanes, with cycloalkanes and aromatic compounds, plus small amounts of compounds containing sulfur, nitrogen and oxygen. It must be separated into fractions before use.

questions.stem: How was petroleum formed?
options: From marine organisms buried in sediment and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years
From volcanic gases that condensed into liquids deep below the sea floor over a few thousand years
From coal that melted when it was heated by the Earth's core over hundreds of millions of years
From carbon dioxide and water that reacted underground in sunlight over millions of years
questions.explanation: The remains of tiny marine organisms such as plankton were buried in mud with little oxygen. Over millions of years, heat and pressure converted the organic matter into the hydrocarbons of petroleum and natural gas.

questions.stem: How does fractional distillation separate crude oil into fractions?
options: The oil is mixed with water, and fractions separate into layers according to how soluble they are in the water
The oil is passed over a catalyst, and fractions form as the large molecules are broken into smaller ones
Vapour rises up a column that is cooler at the top, and fractions condense at the level matching their boiling points
Liquid flows down a column that is hotter at the top, and fractions freeze at the level matching their melting points
questions.explanation: Heated crude oil vapour enters near the bottom of the column. Components with higher boiling points condense lower down, where it is hotter, while those with lower boiling points rise further before condensing. Breaking molecules over a catalyst is cracking, a separate process.

questions.stem: In the fractional distillation of crude oil, where is the fraction with the largest molecules collected?
options: At the top of the column, as refinery gases
In the middle of the column, as petrol
At the top of the column, as kerosene
At the bottom of the column, as bitumen residue
questions.explanation: The largest molecules have the strongest dispersion forces and the highest boiling points, so they do not vaporise and are drawn off at the bottom as residue used for bitumen. The smallest molecules leave at the top as refinery gases.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental impact of burning fuels refined from petroleum, such as petrol and diesel?
options: Release of chlorofluorocarbons, which deplete the ozone layer
Release of oxygen, which raises the risk of bushfires
Release of phosphates, which cause algal blooms in rivers
Release of carbon dioxide, adding to the enhanced greenhouse effect
questions.explanation: Combustion of hydrocarbon fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, along with pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates. CFCs were refrigerants and propellants, not combustion products, and burning consumes oxygen rather than releasing it.

questions.stem: A long-chain alkane is cracked: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + X. What is X?
options: C₂H₂
CH₄
C₂H₄
C₂H₆
questions.explanation: Balancing atoms, X contains 10 − 8 = 2 carbons and 22 − 18 = 4 hydrogens, so it is ethene, C₂H₄. Cracking an alkane usually gives a shorter alkane and an alkene.

questions.stem: Why do refineries crack some of the larger hydrocarbons from fractional distillation?
options: To remove sulfur compounds that would otherwise poison the catalysts
To separate the hydrocarbons again according to their boiling points
To make smaller, more useful molecules, including alkenes such as ethene
To join small molecules into larger ones for heavy fuel oil and bitumen
questions.explanation: Distillation yields more heavy fractions than are needed and less petrol and feedstock. Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes for fuel and alkenes such as ethene, the starting material for many polymers.

questions.stem: Which sequence produces chloroethene, the monomer of PVC, from ethene?
options: Add HCl to give chloroethane, then heat it so that it loses H₂
Substitute Cl for one H of ethene using Cl₂ in UV light, with no other step
Add Cl₂ to give 1,2-dichloroethane, then add H₂ to remove a chlorine atom
Add Cl₂ to give 1,2-dichloroethane, then heat it so that it loses HCl
questions.explanation: Ethene reacts with chlorine in an addition reaction to form CH₂ClCH₂Cl. Heating this to a high temperature eliminates HCl: CH₂ClCH₂Cl → CH₂=CHCl + HCl, regenerating a double bond. Adding H₂ would not create the double bond needed in the monomer.

questions.stem: What is the monomer of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)?
options: Tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂
Tetrafluoroethane, CF₃CHF₂
Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl
Fluoroethene, CH₂=CHF
questions.explanation: PTFE is an addition polymer of tetrafluoroethene, in which all four hydrogens of ethene are replaced by fluorine. A monomer for addition polymerisation must contain a C=C double bond, which tetrafluoroethane lacks.

questions.stem: Which is the repeating unit of polyvinyl chloride (PVC)?
options: -CH₂=CHCl-
-CHCl-CHCl-
-CH₂-CH₂-Cl-
-CH₂-CHCl-
questions.explanation: When chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl, polymerises, its double bond opens, and each unit joins its neighbours by single bonds, keeping one Cl on alternate carbons. The repeating unit has no double bond.

questions.stem: What happens to the C=C bond when ethene undergoes addition polymerisation?
options: The double bond becomes a triple bond, which links the monomers into chains
One bond of the double bond breaks, and each carbon bonds to a neighbouring monomer
The whole double bond breaks, and a water molecule is released for every link
The double bond stays intact, and the monomers are joined by hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation, one of the two bonds in each C=C opens and forms new single bonds to neighbouring monomers, giving a long saturated chain. No small molecule is released; that happens in condensation polymerisation.

questions.stem: PVC is more rigid and has a higher softening temperature than polyethylene. What best explains this?
options: Polar C-Cl bonds give dipole-dipole attractions between PVC chains
PVC chains are joined by covalent cross-links through chlorine atoms
PVC chains form hydrogen bonds through their hydrogen atoms
Polyethylene chains are ionic, so they slide past each other easily
questions.explanation: The C-Cl bond is polar, so dipole-dipole forces act between PVC chains in addition to dispersion forces, holding them together more strongly. PVC is not cross-linked, has no hydrogen bonding, and polyethylene is non-polar, not ionic.

questions.stem: PTFE is used for non-stick cookware coatings and plumber's tape. Which properties suit these uses?
options: It conducts heat and electricity well, like a metal coating
It reacts with fats and oils, breaking them down as food cooks
It is chemically unreactive, heat resistant and has very low friction
It is soluble in water, which lets food and dirt wash off easily
questions.explanation: Strong C-F bonds and a sheath of fluorine atoms around the carbon chain make PTFE very unreactive, stable at cooking temperatures and slippery, so very little sticks to it. It is insoluble in water and is an electrical insulator.

questions.stem: Why is polypropylene, rather than low-density polyethylene, used for food containers that go through a hot dishwasher?
options: It is a condensation polymer, so it is stronger when hot
It is an ionic solid, so it does not melt at any temperature
It softens at a higher temperature, so it keeps its shape
It dissolves in hot water, so it cleans itself in the wash
questions.explanation: Polypropylene has a higher softening and melting temperature than LDPE, so containers made from it stay rigid in hot water. Both are addition polymers that are insoluble in water.

questions.stem: A sample of PVC has an average molar mass of 125 000 g mol⁻¹. The monomer, CH₂=CHCl, has M = 62.50 g mol⁻¹. On average, how many monomer units are in each chain?
questions.explanation: An addition polymer has the same mass per repeating unit as its monomer, because no atoms are lost. 125 000 / 62.50 = 2000 units. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 7.8 × 10⁶.

questions.stem: Why is chloroethene (vinyl chloride) tightly controlled in PVC factories?
options: It is a solid dust that blocks the air filters in the factory
It is a carcinogen that can cause liver cancer in exposed workers
It is a strong acid that dissolves the steel of the reaction vessels
It is radioactive and must be stored behind thick lead shielding
questions.explanation: Long-term exposure to chloroethene gas has been linked to a rare liver cancer in workers, so exposure limits are strict and unreacted monomer is removed from the finished PVC. Chloroethene is a flammable gas, not an acid or a radioactive substance.

questions.stem: Why should waste PVC not be burnt in open fires or simple incinerators?
options: Burning it releases hydrogen chloride and toxic chlorine compounds
Burning it releases fluorine gas, which attacks the ozone layer
It explodes when heated, because each chain stores a double bond
It turns into chloroethene gas, which then forms acid rain clouds
questions.explanation: PVC contains a large proportion of chlorine, so burning it releases corrosive hydrogen chloride gas and can form toxic chlorinated compounds such as dioxins. It contains no fluorine, and the polymer chains have no double bonds.

questions.stem: Which is an environmental concern associated with PTFE?
options: It breaks down in sunlight into fluorine gas within weeks
It dissolves in rivers, making the water strongly acidic
It releases chloroethene when it is used for cooking
Some fluorinated chemicals used in making it are very persistent
questions.explanation: PTFE itself is extremely unreactive and does not biodegrade, and some fluorinated processing chemicals used in its production persist for a very long time in the environment and in living things. Overheated non-stick pans can also release harmful fumes. PTFE is insoluble and contains no chlorine.

questions.stem: Why do discarded polyethylene and polypropylene items cause long-term harm in the oceans?
options: They sink and react with sediments to form crude oil again
They do not biodegrade, so they persist and break into microplastics
They dissolve in sea water and make it toxic to marine animals
They react with salt to release chlorine gas into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: These polymers are non-polar hydrocarbon chains that microorganisms cannot readily break down. They persist for many years, harming animals that eat or become entangled in them, and slowly fragment into microplastics.

questions.stem: Dorothy Hodgkin determined the structures of penicillin and vitamin B₁₂. Which evidence did she use?
options: Flame tests and atomic emission spectra of the compounds
X-ray crystallography of crystals of the compounds
Proton NMR spectra of the compounds in solution
Mass spectra of the compounds and their fragments
questions.explanation: Hodgkin used the diffraction patterns produced when X-rays pass through crystals to calculate the positions of the atoms in these medicinal compounds. She was awarded the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

questions.stem: A ¹³C NMR spectrum shows a peak at about 125 ppm. Which carbon environment does this indicate?
options: A carbon in a C=C double bond
A carbon in a CH₃ group
A carbon bonded to an OH group
A carbon in a C≡C triple bond
questions.explanation: Alkene carbons typically appear between about 110 and 150 ppm. A CH₃ carbon appears at low shift (roughly 8 to 25 ppm), a C-OH carbon at about 50 to 90 ppm, and alkyne carbons at about 75 to 95 ppm.

questions.stem: How many peaks appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The molecule is symmetrical about carbon 3, so the two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, as are the two CH₂ carbons, and the CH(OH) carbon is unique. That gives three carbon environments and three peaks.

questions.stem: A compound C₄H₁₀O has a broad IR absorption at 3230 to 3550 cm⁻¹ and only two peaks in its ¹³C NMR spectrum. What is it?
options: 2-methylpropan-2-ol
Butan-1-ol
Butan-2-ol
2-methylpropan-1-ol
questions.explanation: The broad IR band shows an alcohol O-H. In (CH₃)₃COH the three methyl carbons are equivalent and the central carbon is unique, giving two peaks. Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol each give four peaks, and 2-methylpropan-1-ol gives three.

questions.stem: In the high resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-chloropropane, CH₃CHClCH₃, how are the signals split?
options: A 3H doublet and a 3H septet
A 6H doublet and a 1H septet
A 6H septet and a 1H doublet
A 6H triplet and a 1H quartet
questions.explanation: The six CH₃ hydrogens are equivalent and each has one neighbouring H, so by the n + 1 rule they give a doublet. The single CH hydrogen has six neighbouring H, so it gives a septet (seven lines). The areas are in the ratio 6 : 1.

questions.stem: Why is tetramethylsilane (TMS) added as a reference in ¹H NMR spectroscopy?
options: It removes water from the sample so that no O-H peak appears
Its 12 equivalent hydrogens give one sharp peak, set at 0 ppm
It reacts with the sample so that every hydrogen can be detected
Its hydrogens give a peak at a higher shift than any organic compound
questions.explanation: TMS, Si(CH₃)₄, is unreactive and all 12 hydrogens are in the same environment, giving a single strong peak that is defined as 0 ppm. Its peak lies at a lower shift than almost all other hydrogens, so it does not overlap with the sample's signals.

questions.stem: How many different hydrogen environments are in propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: The CH₃, the middle CH₂, the CH₂ bonded to oxygen and the OH hydrogen are each in a different environment, so the low resolution ¹H NMR spectrum shows four peaks. Counting individual hydrogen atoms gives 8, which is not the number of environments.

questions.stem: An ester C₃H₆O₂ gives two ¹H NMR peaks: 3.7 ppm (3H, singlet) and 2.0 ppm (3H, singlet). Which compound is it?
options: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH
Methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃
Methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃
Ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃
questions.explanation: Two singlets of 3H each mean two CH₃ groups with no neighbouring H. The CH₃ bonded to the ester oxygen appears near 3.7 ppm and the CH₃ next to C=O near 2.0 ppm. Ethyl methanoate would show a quartet and triplet, and methyl propanoate has the formula C₄H₈O₂.

questions.stem: A compound C₂H₄O₂ gives ¹H NMR peaks at 11.5 ppm (1H, singlet) and 2.1 ppm (3H, singlet), and an IR band at 2500 to 3000 cm⁻¹. What is it?
options: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃
Ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH₂CH₂OH
questions.explanation: A 1H singlet at 10 to 13 ppm and a very broad IR band at 2500 to 3000 cm⁻¹ are typical of a carboxylic acid O-H, and the 3H singlet at 2.1 ppm is a CH₃ next to C=O. Methyl methanoate is an isomer, but its CH₃ bonded to oxygen would appear near 3.7 ppm and it has no O-H.
